newsitem.title: USA: US government pays $3.5 bln a year for electricity.
newsitem.headline: US government pays $3.5 bln a year for electricity.

text.p: The U.S. government annually spends about $3.5 billion on electricity, of which half is for military facilities, according to a General Accounting Office report released Monday.

The report by the Congressional watchdog agency was done for Republicans Rep. Thomas Bliley of Virginia and Rep. Dan Schaefer of Colorado who are leading the House's effort to deregulate local power markets.
The two lawmakers asked GAO to do a follow-up study on how much the government would save if power markets were open to competition.

From 1986 to 1995, the latest year for which information was available, the annual electric bill at federal buildings and facilities was steady at about $3.5 billion, while electricity use rose from 0.16 quadrillion BTUs to 0.21 quads.
Six agencies, including the Defense Department and the Tennessee Valley Authority, accounted for 87 percent of annual electricity costs, the report said.
Other energy costs for the government fell by $900 million to $1.0 billion a year from 1986 to 1995.
